enrichment.short_title: Prison inquest neglect rider after Middleton
key_facts: Sheena Creamer, a remand prisoner at HMP New Hall, hanged herself in August 2000 after a locum doctor discharged her from the healthcare centre despite an open F2052SH self-harm form.
The coroner’s jury returned a majority suicide verdict without a neglect rider, though the coroner later made a Rule 43 report about the doctor’s lack of understanding of F2052SH procedures.
The deceased’s mother, Helen Sacker, sought judicial review to quash the inquisition and order a fresh inquest.
Tucker J refused permission on delay and merits; the Court of Appeal applied Middleton on Article 2 and the neglect rider.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal with appeal to follow against refusal of permission to apply for judicial review of a coroner’s inquest decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; time extended, permission granted, inquisition quashed, and fresh inquest ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Following Middleton, where systemic neglect could reduce the risk of repetition of deaths in custody, a coroner should leave the jury the opportunity to add a neglect rider to a suicide verdict if a clear causal connection exists; Rule 43 action alone does not satisfy Article 2, and delay was excusable where Middleton post-dated the inquest.
legal_issues: Whether the coroner should have left the jury the opportunity to add a neglect rider after Middleton
Whether alleged failures in F2052SH procedures had the necessary causal connection to the death
Whether Rule 43 reporting satisfied the Article 2 investigative duty
Whether time to bring judicial review should be extended
linked_authorities: R (Amin) v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R v HM Coroner for North Humberside and Scunthorpe ex p Jamieson
R v Stratford-upon-Avon District Council ex parte Jackson

confidence.notes: Full appellate judgment with clear outcome, statutory framework, and explicit application of Middleton.

enrichment.short_title: Trade mark appeal costs split by issue
key_facts: After the substantive appeal in a trade mark dispute over ESB beer registration, Fuller’s appealed the trial judge’s order that each party bear its own costs.
The judge had treated the case as involving distinct non-use and distinctiveness issues and effectively set off costs between them.
Most costs were incurred on distinctiveness, on which the defendants succeeded, while the claimant succeeded only on a limited non-use point.
The claimant had not beaten a without-prejudice save as to costs offer dated 31 August 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on costs following determination of the substantive trade mark appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Costs appeal allowed; Fuller's to recover 80% of costs at trial, their costs of the costs appeal, and 65% of costs of the substantive appeal and cross-appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties succeed on clearly distinct issues under CPR 44, costs should be allocated issue-by-issue according to relative importance and expenditure; a no-order-as-to-costs outcome is wrong when the majority of costs related to the issue on which the paying party succeeded, and Calderbank-style offers either beat the judgment or do not assist on costs.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge erred in making no order as to costs
Whether costs should be apportioned between non-use and distinctiveness issues
Whether correspondence beyond an admissible offer could be considered on costs
Whether reserved interlocutory costs should remain costs in the case

confidence.notes: Judgment concerns costs only; substantive trade mark outcome is background but costs reasoning is explicit.

key_facts: Express Dairies’ milk tanker spilled about 4,000 litres of milk into Battlefield Brook after a tyre blow-out caused a chain of damage on the M5.
The driver pulled onto the hard shoulder near unprotected drains feeding controlled waters; milk entered the brook and a pond at Silverdale.
Magistrates convicted Express of causing polluting matter to enter controlled waters and rejected the section 89 emergency defence.
On case stated appeal, the company accepted milk was polluting matter and the brook was controlled waters.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates’ conviction for water pollution.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed unless the Environment Agency applied within 14 days to remit for further hearing on remaining section 89 limbs; defendant's costs order made.
enrichment.ratio: Where polluting matter enters controlled waters because the driver pulled onto the hard shoulder in an emergency to avoid danger to life or health, section 89(1)(a) may apply to the act that caused the entry even if earlier events in the chain were not emergencies; tyre blow-outs and subsequent tanker damage were not extraordinary enough to break causation under Empress Car principles.
legal_issues: Whether the chain of causation was broken by extraordinary events
Whether section 89(1) applies when entry results from emergency action rather than the discharge itself being the emergency
Whether Article 14 required a broader construction of section 89
Whether there was evidence the defendant caused the entry
linked_authorities: Environment Agency v Empress Car Company (Abertillery) Ltd
de Freitas v Permanent Secretary of Ministry of Agriculture Fisheries, Lands and Housing

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on causation and statutory defence with clear stated-case answers.

enrichment.short_title: Pensions ombudsman JR on procedural fairness

statutes_considered.title: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Transitional Provisions) (Ombudsman Scheme and Complaints Scheme) Order 2001

key_facts: Independent financial adviser Mr Green advised Mrs Waring in 1993 not to join her employer’s Courtaulds occupational pension scheme and to continue a personal pension plan.
The Financial Ombudsman found the advice non-compliant with Pensions Review Guidance and inappropriate, ordering loss assessment and redress.
Mr Green challenged the decision for procedural unfairness and material mistake of fact about transfer value components.
The ombudsman accepted a mistake about contributions equivalent premiums but said it was immaterial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of a Financial Ombudsman decision on a transitional PIAOB complaint.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal refused (28 days to renew application); defendant's costs to detailed assessment with limited order on supplemental witness statement costs.
enrichment.ratio: An ombudsman need not itemise every scheme benefit before deciding appropriateness if the adviser and solicitors knew the Pensions Review Guidance and were asked for further representations after interim findings and scheme information; an immaterial error of fact about a minor transfer-value component does not render the decision liable to quashing.
legal_issues: Whether procedural fairness required the ombudsman to specify every benefit relied on
Whether the ombudsman’s mistake about CEP/time value was material
Whether mistake of fact is a separate ground of judicial review
Whether transitional PIAOB criteria applied
linked_authorities: R (Alconbury Developments Ltd) v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions
R (McLellan) v Bracknell Forest Borough Council
Begum v London Borough of Tower Hamlets

confidence.notes: Long judgment with detailed procedural history and explicit findings on fairness and immaterial error.

enrichment.short_title: IT contract preliminary issue on benchmarking
key_facts: Cable & Wireless and IBM disputed construction of Schedule 10 to a Global Framework Agreement on retrospective price adjustments after Compass benchmarking reports.
IBM contended the Compass reports were invalid; C&W sought a preliminary trial on the construction of paragraph 5.3 alone.
Colman J had refused a preliminary issue in December 2002 but circumstances changed when IBM dropped rectification and estoppel pleas.
A full trial was estimated at 8–10 weeks and could not start before January 2004, while the construction issue might take 3–4 days.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case management conference application to revisit an order refusing trial of a preliminary issue.
enrichment.outcome: Construction issue ordered to be tried as a preliminary issue on an expedited basis; directions given for that trial and remaining issues.
enrichment.ratio: Where circumstances have materially changed—especially removal of rectification and estoppel, a discrete short construction issue, and imminent further benchmarking under a long-term contract—it is appropriate to order a preliminary issue trial even if a full trial remains necessary on other questions.
legal_issues: Whether the construction of GFA Schedule 10 paragraph 5.3 should be tried as a preliminary issue
Whether changed pleadings and trial length justified revisiting Colman J’s case management decision
How to manage Compass benchmarking validity issues alongside the counterclaim

confidence.notes: Procedural case management judgment with clear reasoning; no substantive construction holding.

key_facts: Mrs Grace on a motorcycle and Mrs Tanner in a car collided on the A23 when Tanner missed the correct roundabout exit and continued round while Grace assumed she would leave on the dual carriageway.
The county court judge found Tanner wholly blameless, holding Grace failed to keep a proper lookout and made a dangerous assumption.
Tanner had remained in the inside lane without sudden movements after realising she had missed the A23 exit.
The Court of Appeal held Tanner should have looked for traffic on the outside lane intending to take the dual carriageway exit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court judgment on liability in a road traffic accident.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; liability apportioned 50/50; matter remitted to county court; defendant to pay 75% of trial costs and all appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Missing a roundabout exit is not necessarily negligent, but once a driver passes an exit and continues round knowing another dual carriageway exit exists, failing to check for traffic in the outside lane that may intend to use that exit is negligent and can justify equal apportionment with a motorcyclist who also acted carelessly.
legal_issues: Whether missing a roundabout exit was negligent
When a duty arose to look for traffic in the outside lane
Whether the judge erred in finding sole liability on the motorcyclist
Application of Highway Code paragraphs 162–163

confidence.notes: Short factual judgment with unanimous Court of Appeal reasoning and clear apportionment order.

key_facts: ABCI claimed it had subscribed for shares in Tunisian bank BFT in 1982 but BFT refused to issue shares and froze its payment.

Long-running English proceedings against BFT, STB, BCT and the Tunisian Ministry of Finance were set aside for want of jurisdiction and, as to the MOF, defective service under the State Immunity Act 1978.
The judge ordered indemnity costs and interest on costs from December 2000 at 8%.
The Court of Appeal upheld jurisdiction/set-aside decisions and indemnity costs but varied interest on costs to 1% over base rate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Commercial Court decisions setting aside service out of the jurisdiction, upholding state immunity/service points, and making costs orders.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed except costs interest varied from 8% to 1% over base rate; standard-basis costs payable within 56 days.
enrichment.ratio: No good arguable case was shown that 1982 contractual documents were authentic or that tort jurisdiction under O.11 r.1(1)(f) was established; indemnity costs were justified by the claimant’s changing case, curative jurisdiction applications, and voluminous litigation conduct, but pre-judgment interest on costs is discretionary and not limited to the Judgments Act rate.
legal_issues: Whether English jurisdiction existed over Tunisian bank and state defendants
Whether service complied with the State Immunity Act 1978
Whether indemnity costs were properly awarded
Whether separate representation costs for related defendants were reasonable
What rate of pre-judgment interest on costs was permissible
linked_authorities: Domicrest Ltd v Swiss Bank Corporation
Amoco (UK) Exploration Co v British American Offshore Ltd

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; core jurisdiction, immunity, and costs holdings are clear though factual background is complex.

enrichment.short_title: Section 41 refusal and rape sentence reduction

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Singh was convicted at retrial of two rapes and one attempted rape against two women in 1997, after his first conviction was quashed because a complainant had falsely claimed virginity.
Defence counsel applied under section 41 to cross-examine the second complainant on prior sexual intercourse with another man and to call supporting witnesses; the judge refused.
The prosecution did not rely on virginity at the second trial.
Singh received 19 years total (7 plus 12 consecutive plus concurrent terms) at sentencing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction and appeal against sentence following retrial.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to appeal against conviction refused; sentence appeal partly allowed—second rape term reduced from 12 to 8 years, total sentence 15 years.
enrichment.ratio: Evidence of a complainant’s sexual intercourse with a third party to undermine credibility falls within section 41 and requires leave under section 41(2), which cannot be granted where section 41(4) blocks use aimed at impugning credibility and section 41(5) does not apply without prosecution reliance on virginity; consecutive sentences totalling 19 years were excessive though individual terms were not.
legal_issues: Whether section 41 permitted cross-examination about prior sexual behaviour and false virginity evidence
Whether the evidence went to a non-consent issue rather than credibility
Whether trial counsel failed to advance the correct section 41 application
Whether the total sentence was excessive
index_terms: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999
R v T; R v H
linked_authorities: R v T; R v H

confidence.notes: Focused criminal appeal with detailed section 41 analysis and explicit sentence variation.

enrichment.short_title: Film finance reinsurance Stabler warranty breach
key_facts: Reinsurers of New Hampshire’s 60% line on a $118.75m contingency policy covering noteholder default by film company Destination sought declarations of non-liability.
The reinsurance slip required Steve Stabler’s employment contract as CEO to be maintained for the policy period; Stabler left Destination on 8 November 1999.
The insurance policy and Operating Agreement contained different employment provisions; Great Lakes reinsurer had not seen all underlying documents.
Willis admitted broker duties and liability if reinsurers succeeded; New Hampshire counterclaimed and sued Willis as Part 20 defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of consolidated reinsurance coverage disputes.
enrichment.outcome: Reinsurers held not liable under the reinsurance slip; New Hampshire entitled to damages from broker Willis without contributory negligence reduction.
enrichment.ratio: The Stabler Wording in the reinsurance slip was an express warranty requiring maintenance of Stabler’s employment for the policy period, not merely incorporation of Operating Agreement terms; its breach discharged reinsurers, and the retention provision did not oblige New Hampshire to retain 20% in the strict sense alleged.
legal_issues: Construction of the Stabler employment condition in the reinsurance slip
Whether the Stabler Wording was a warranty or reflected the Operating Agreement only
Construction of the 20% retention provision
Whether New Hampshire contributorily negligent in failing to query slip wording
linked_authorities: HIH Casualty and General Insurance Ltd v New Hampshire Insurance Co
Groupama Navigation et Aérienne v Catatumbo
ICS Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society

confidence.notes: Detailed coverage judgment with agreed facts and clear warranty construction holding.

enrichment.short_title: Lost replacement job damages after RTA
key_facts: Sharon Morris lost her radiographer job because of injuries from a road accident caused by Mr Clifford (appealed as Richards).
She obtained higher-paid work at Toshiba but resigned in November 2000 alleging discrimination, remaining unemployed at trial in October 2001.
The judge found she could have found alternative work at £17,500 and awarded future loss including the period after leaving Toshiba.
The defendant argued post-Toshiba losses were too remote or reflected failure to mitigate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against assessment of special damages for future loss of earnings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; damages for the period after leaving Toshiba upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tort victim loses employment because of the defendant’s wrong and takes reasonable steps to mitigate by accepting a new job that fails because she lacks the required capabilities, she may recover continuing loss of earnings unless she was at fault in losing that job; the question is one of justice rather than rigid remoteness/mitigation categorisation.
legal_issues: Whether loss after resignation from Toshiba was too remote
Whether the issue was mitigation or remoteness of damage
Whether there was evidence the claimant was unsuited to the Toshiba job
Burden of proof on mitigation

confidence.notes: Appellate judgment with clear fact-specific findings on suitability for replacement employment.
